draft.title: Gene flow
card: Gene flow is the movement of alleles from one population to another. It happens when individuals migrate and then breed in the new population.
Moving is not enough. If the migrant does not breed, no alleles pass into the new gene pool and there is no gene flow.
Gene flow can add alleles that were missing from a population. It can also change the frequency of alleles that were already there.
Gene flow tends to make two populations more alike. Where it is blocked, such as by a barrier, the populations can become more different over time.
draft.remember: Gene flow needs migration and breeding, and it makes populations more alike.

a.q: Which event is an example of gene flow?
opts: A bird flies to a new island and breeds with local birds
A bird flies to a new island and dies without breeding
A storm kills most of the birds on an island
A bird on an island gains a new allele by mutation
a.why: Gene flow needs alleles to enter another population's gene pool, which happens only if the migrant breeds there. A migrant that dies without breeding adds no alleles, so that option is the tempting wrong one.
a.clue: Alleles must pass into the new gene pool.

b.q: Two populations of wildflowers grow on either side of a farm. Bees carry pollen between them each spring. What is the likely effect on the two populations over time?
opts: They become more alike in allele frequencies
They become more different in allele frequencies
They each lose all of their existing alleles
They stop changing in allele frequencies altogether
b.why: Pollen carried by bees moves alleles between the populations, and this is gene flow. Gene flow tends to make populations more alike. Blocking it, not allowing it, would let the populations drift apart.
b.clue: Think about what moving alleles between populations does to the differences between them.

a.best: A bird flies to a new island and breeds with local birds

b.best: They become more alike in allele frequencies

problems.detail: The card defines gene flow as individuals migrating and then breeding. Pollen carried by bees is gametes moving, not individuals migrating. A student working only from the card may doubt that this counts as gene flow; the card should mention that gametes such as pollen can carry alleles between populations.
The remember line says gene flow 'makes populations more alike', but the card says it 'tends to make' them more alike. Dropping the hedge overstates the effect.

The why says blocking gene flow would let the populations 'drift apart'. 'Drift' could be confused with genetic drift, a separate point in this chapter. The card says the populations 'can become more different'.
